answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: From Mill’s Autobiography (Chapter 5, “A Crisis in My Mental History”), published posthumously in 1873. The line is confirmed verbatim in the primary text, where it states his “anti-self-consciousness” view — the paradox that happiness pursued directly slips away.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Ch. 5, “A Crisis in My Mental History. One Stage Onward”

source.excerpt: They will not bear a scrutinizing examination. Ask yourself whether you are happy, and you cease to be so. The only chance is to treat, not happiness, but some end external to it, as the purpose of life.
trail: The line appears verbatim in Mill’s Autobiography, Chapter 5, in the passage on his recovery from his mental crisis.
Independently confirmed in the University of Texas transcription of Autobiography, Chapter 5, with identical wording and punctuation.
The Autobiography was published in 1873, the year of Mill’s death, placing the text firmly in the public domain.
source.excerptNote: Mill is describing the theory of life he adopted after his mental crisis of 1826–27: that the “enjoyments of life … are sufficient … when they are taken en passant, without being made a principal object,” but collapse the moment they are made the direct aim.
source.rightsNote: Mill’s Autobiography was first published in 1873, well before the 1931 cutoff, so the English text is in the public domain in the United States.

author.name: John Stuart Mill
author.heading: About John Stuart Mill
author.metaLine: 1806–1873 · English philosopher, political economist & Member of Parliament
author.bio: John Stuart Mill was the leading English-language philosopher of the 19th century, a defender of individual liberty, utilitarian ethics, and women’s suffrage. Raised on an intense, isolating education engineered by his father James Mill, he suffered a famous depressive crisis in his early twenties that reshaped his thinking about happiness. His Autobiography (1873), On Liberty (1859), and Utilitarianism (1861) remain central texts of liberal thought.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: The sentence sits at the heart of Mill’s account of his mental breakdown. Trained from infancy to be a reasoning machine for utilitarian reform, he asked himself around 1826 whether achieving all his goals would make him happy — and an “irrepressible self-consciousness distinctly answered, ‘No!’” The crisis nearly undid him.

His way out was what he later found echoed in Carlyle: the “anti-self-consciousness theory.” Those are happiest, Mill concluded, whose minds are fixed on some end other than their own happiness — happiness is caught obliquely, “by the way,” never by direct pursuit. The line is the classic English statement of what philosophers call the paradox of hedonism.
